Seminar Title:

Glycosylation Effects on the Stability and Aggregation of Peptides and Proteins: A Computer Simulation Study

Seminar Type:

Progress Seminar

Department:

Chemistry

Speaker Name:

Bilash Maity ( Rollno : 523cy1001)

Speaker Type:

Student

Venue:

Seminar Hall, Chemistry Department

Date and Time:

25 Sep 2026 4:30 PM

Contact:

Madhurima Jana

Abstract:

Aggregation or self-assembly is a common but unwanted process that alters the pharmacokinetic properties of peptides and proteins. On the other hand, protein stability is an essential parameter in therapeutic development. Aggregation generally occurs through the noncovalent association of polypeptide chains. Such a phenomenon reduces the physical stability of peptides and proteins, creating toxicity and immunogenicity. Therefore, preventive measures are needed to inhibit such processes. Glycosylation, a post-translational modification involving the attachment of sugar moieties to proteins, has been shown to enhance protein stability and prevent aggregation. However, controversy exists on its effects on proteins. In this work, molecular dynamics simulations and network analyses were used to investigate the effects of glycosylation on peptide aggregation and protein stability. In The effects of glycosylation of a peptide fragment of insulin, a sequence known for its amyloid-like fibril formation was glycosylated with single mannose and di-mannose, and their aggregation propensity was investigated using atomistic molecular dynamics (MD) simulations by using additive and polarizable Drude force fields. Transition network analysis confirmed a shift toward smaller oligomers as glycosylation increased. Although both force fields showed the same aggregation trend, they produced distinct aggregate morphologies, highlighting the role of electronic polarization. We further investigated the effects of glycosylation on insulin monomers by attaching mannose at multiple sites in different combinations at both physiological (300K) and elevated (400K) temperatures. Finally, di-mannosylation of Chignolin was investigated under denaturing conditions at various urea concentrations. We believe our findings will provide insights into the stabilizing and aggregation-inhibitory effects of glycosylation and its potential role in preventing fibrillation, contributing to the development of improved protein formulations for therapeutic treatments.
